label: the single-flight gate is dropped, so two publishes of one site open two sandboxes — two bills, and two artifacts racing to be the one that deploys

each enqueue reuses a deterministic per-site job id, so arq silently REFUSES every rebuild for as long as the previous job's result lives in Redis (an hour by default) — a single-flight guard nobody asked for, in the wrong layer

a settlement of 'stay in flight' writes a status anyway, so a retryable failure lands terminal between attempts — should_enqueue reads that as free to re-publish and a second sandbox starts on top of the retry

the engine gate accepts anything, so html (whose output IS the project root) reaches a sandbox: the include-list tar cannot exclude node_modules from it, and the build is billed before artifact_tar_command refuses it
an empty scaffold is no longer detected, so a sandbox is created, installed and billed to build nothing — and the empty-deploy failure is caught (if at all) only after the money is spent
node_modules stops being pruned from the uploaded tree, so a scaffold that shares a directory with a previous install puts ~500 MB on the wire per build

the wrong directory is uploaded (the generator's out dir instead of the projectDir it returns), so every source file lands one level deeper than the build config expects and the build fails for a reason nothing in the lane can explain

the arq function timeout is hard-coded to the shared workspace-jobs budget, so arq cancels a long build BEFORE the in-sandbox timeout(1) fires: no sentinel is written and a healthy-but-slow build is recorded as lost infrastructure

the sandbox is held to a budget re-derived from the environment instead of the one the enqueue measured its staleness window against, so a config change mid-flight leaves a live build outside its own window and it gets re-enqueued on top of itself
an unreachable Daytona re-raises WITHOUT recording anything, so the row stays in 'building' until the staleness window lapses and every publish in between is a silent no-op

label: the row never flips to 'building', so a queued build and a running one are indistinguishable — which is the exact distinction 'queued' was added for, and what turns a concurrency cap into support tickets

the queued->building flip stops re-stamping the clock, so the attempt's staleness window is spent on queue wait: a build that waited behind the cap is declared stale while it is still running, and re-enqueued on top of itself

the outcome write becomes a full save() instead of a targeted set, so a minutes-long build finishing writes its whole stale snapshot back and silently reverts a publish that landed while it ran — a live site pointed at its old URL, with nothing in any log
